blocks.text: The case in brief

The Western Cape can grow international arrivals from about 1.5 million in 2025 to 2.2 million by 2035 on the base path, and to 2.5 million on the accelerated path. Gateway capacity sets the pace in the summer peak; demand and conversion set it in the green season and beyond the Metro.

From 1,498,829 arrivals in 2025 the growth model reaches 2,175,778 on the base path and 2,516,282 on the accelerated path in 2035 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20). International passenger arrivals at Cape Town International, the series ACSA reports, stood at 1.44m in FY24/25 and 1.57m in FY25/26 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11).

The study tested an eighteen-entry hypothesis tree against seven deliverables and four working analyses between December 2025 and October 2026. This report sets out what the evidence found, what Wesgro and its partners should do and how progress will be measured.
Five constraints cap the case

items: **The gateway.** The growth model draws current air access as a line at 1.8 million inbound seats, and the base case crosses it around 2030. Runway relief is planned for about 2033, though ACSA now schedules the realigned runway for December 2029 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21; Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p103; ACSA, Q1 2026/27 presentation to the Portfolio Committee on Transport, as reported by Travel News, Aug 2026).

**Full routes.** Eleven of 27 tabled international routes run above 80% load, and carriers on full routes raise fares before they add seats (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, Seasonality; In Conclusion).

**Seasons.** June holds 6.4% of the year's international seats, and about 62% of overseas visitor travel falls between October and March (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, Seasonality; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12).
**Reach.** Accessibility falls from 4.7 out of 5 in the Cape Metro to 1.0 in the Central Karoo, and one touring route of six is rated Ready (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88 to p90, p30).

**Levers held elsewhere.** Visas, air service agreements and the airport and port programmes sit with national government and SOEs, and no approved method exists for provincial tourism GDP and jobs (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58; Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p103, p112; Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p37).

blocks.text: Strategy on a page

The updated hypothesis tree holds three pillars, six themes and twenty focus areas. Ten focus areas carried through as Validated and six were reworded to the lever the evidence supports. Of the other four, one was refined, one is new, one moved between pillars and one is flagged for analysis still to be commissioned.

blocks.text: How the tree changed since December

Eight December entries changed scope, place or form, and one focus area was added. The changes point the same way: from general ambitions to the specific lever the evidence supports, and from provincial supply to national escalation where the lever sits nationally.

Nine changes turned eighteen December entries into twenty focus areas, each driven by a named workstream. The air access and cruise entry split in two: focus area 7, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes, is Reworded, and focus area 8, Grow cruise calls and ports, is New. Focus area 19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits, keeps its December title but moves from supply to governance. Focus area 20, Develop workforce and service skills, was added and is Flagged, untested.

Five entries were Reworded to the lever the evidence supports. Develop the Seasonality and Spread Proposition became focus area 2, Create green-season demand with MICE and events. Facilitate Adoption Along the Path to Purchase became focus area 3, Make the whole province findable and bookable. Pivot to Growth Markets (China, India, ME, ASEAN) became focus area 4, Convert India and China hub traffic. Ensure Sustainable Destination Management became focus area 14, Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism. Review Institutional Arrangements (Wesgro, DEDAT, CTT) became focus area 16, Align institutional stakeholders across all three tiers. Drive Community and SME Inclusion became focus area 13, Embed local destination bodies for community inclusion, Refined and held at concept level (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p64; dispositions as recorded at the 14 October 2026 review; section 1.4).
Twenty focus areas

Each focus area below carries the one-sentence finding that opens its Chapter 3 entry, unchanged. The entry itself gives the December hypothesis, the evidence with page references, the recommendation split between Wesgro, its partners and the national tier, a benchmark precedent and the initiative and indicators it leads to.

blocks.caption: Pillar 1: Reshape demand
blocks.source: Chapter 3 toplines, quoted verbatim; dispositions as recorded at the 14 October 2026 review. Sources for each figure are in the Chapter 3 entry.

columns.header: What the evidence shows and what follows

rows: 1 Respond to growth segment traveller preferences
Four traveller segments, each concentrated in named home markets, give Wesgro a sharper target than country alone, and the province scores 3.7 to 4.6 out of 5 on its ability to win them.
2 Create green-season demand with MICE and events

The green season is a seat problem and an events problem at once. June holds 6.4% of the year's international seats, and business events are the lever best placed to fill the trough, though international meetings now peak from September to November.
3 Make the whole province findable and bookable
Outside the Cape Peninsula, the Winelands and the Garden Route, most product cannot be booked where travellers book, so interest the province has already earned has nowhere to land.
4 Convert India and China hub traffic

About 101,000 Indian and Chinese travellers a year already reach Cape Town, mainly through Gulf and African hubs, and with no direct Indian route likely before 2030, converting that flow is the lever available now.
The mature markets already pay the most and fill the fullest routes, so growth there comes from more value per visitor and more seats on existing routes, not from more marketing.
Regional Africa is the province's steadiest volume and its least developed premium market: Zimbabwe and Namibia supply 62% of African arrivals, while West African visitors spend the most per visit.
blocks.message: Conversion, not awareness, holds back the growth markets, the green season and the province beyond its core.

blocks.caption: Pillar 2: Transform supply
blocks.source: Chapter 3 toplines, quoted verbatim; dispositions as recorded at the 14 October 2026 review. Sources for each figure are in the Chapter 3 entry.

columns.header: What the evidence shows and what follows

rows: 7 Win direct routes and add seats on full routes
Eleven of 27 international routes run above 80% load and carriers raise fares before seats, so the province must win frequency and larger aircraft now, ahead of runway relief in about 2033.
Cruise already brings about R1.79bn a year with Cape Town's berth at about 40% of its season capacity, so growth comes from ships, excursions and regional day stops, not from port capital.
Accessibility falls from 4.7 out of 5 in the Cape Metro to 1.0 in the Central Karoo, and beyond the Metro and the Garden Route the province is effectively car-only.
10 Support diversified route and product development

The province does not lack attractions; it lacks finished experiences around them, with assets outside the Metro left without guides, interpretation or bookable product and one touring route of six rated Ready.
The province offers luxury estates and basic self-catering with no mid-scale branded tier between them, and service, interpretation and language readiness thin out with distance from Cape Town.
Boulders is near carrying capacity and Cableway queues reach three hours, so growth at the flagship nature sites must come from managing flows and steering visitors to under-marketed reserves.
blocks.message: The gateway binds first, and beyond the Metro the product exists but is hard to reach, book or stay in.

blocks.caption: Pillar 3: Build enabling capability
blocks.source: Chapter 3 toplines, quoted verbatim; dispositions as recorded at the 14 October 2026 review. Sources for each figure are in the Chapter 3 entry.

columns.header: What the evidence shows and what follows

rows: 13 Embed local destination bodies for community inclusion

Twenty communities hold 18.4% of the province's residents but receive only a small documented share of foreign direct spend, and in eleven the binding constraint is organisation, not distance or product.
14 Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism
Climate is already costing the province sites, routes and revenue, while the local tourism bodies that would manage the response depend on municipal funding that MFMA Circular No. 131 has disrupted.
15 Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies

The province has a capital pipeline for airports, ports, roads and rail, but none of it reaches tourism product, bookability, accommodation depth or community assets, which is where the growth case needs investment.
16 Align institutional stakeholders across all three tiers

Air service agreements and visas sit with national government, mandates are split across three tiers and the national marketing body is under strain, so the province needs one shared agenda with clear decision rights.

Fifteen of the sixteen organisations engaged raised collaboration, and the channels already exist in JAMS, the bid teams and the tour-operator forums, so the task is to turn existing forums into one joint plan.
18 Expedite tourism-enabling policy and data sharing

No approved method exists for provincial tourism GDP and jobs, operators cannot see their own customers and four arrivals measures run unreconciled, so a data-sharing protocol is the precondition for every target.
19 Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits

Visas, air rights, the runway and policing sit with national government, so the province leads by escalation backed with evidence, and delivers the safety programmes and basic services that are its own.
The 300,000 tourism-linked jobs ambition has no baseline and no labour analysis behind it, so the first step is to commission that analysis, and the skills plan follows from it.
blocks.message: Inclusion, capital, governance and data are thin, and several levers sit with national government.

blocks.text: The growth case and its sequence

The three paths differ by intervention, not by demand potential (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p19). The base path needs hub carriers to keep adding capacity and Wesgro's programmes to expand. The accelerated path also needs direct India and China routes and dedicated activation in India, China, the USA and the Gulf; without confirmed routes, volume reverts to base (p19, p20). On the eleven full routes, marketing cannot make up for missing seats, because carriers raise fares instead (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, In Conclusion). On the hub routes, which run at 65% to 72% load and add the most base-case arrivals, it can ("Seasonality").

blocks.caption: Arrivals paths to 2035
blocks.source: Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19 (2025 base); Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20, p21. The 2031 base value and the accelerated and conservative milestones are computed (section 5.3).

callout.text: Only the accelerated path clears 2.5m by 2035; the base path crosses the seat line before 2031.

blocks.text: Air access and bookability move first, because every other lever runs through them. Phase 1, Activate (2027 to 2028), holds and adds seats on the full routes, builds the green-season calendar and counts and closes the bookability gap. It also starts two or three inclusion pilots and sets up Steerco, the data protocol and the national escalation agenda. Phase 2, Expand (2029 to 2031), scales what works and meets the model's seat line at the 2030 mid-term review. Phase 3, Sustain (2032 to 2035), takes the direct route cases to carriers as runway capacity arrives.

Eighteen initiatives carry the plan, one per focus area except where one owner delivers two. Wesgro is accountable for twelve; DEDAT, the Department of Mobility, municipalities and site operators lead the other six. Thirteen draw mainly on Wesgro's operating budget. None has yet been costed, and setting the rand bands is the first funding task (section 4.6).
The first 24 months

Twelve actions can start in the first 24 months, nine of them inside Wesgro's current mandate and budget. Each opens a seat, a baseline or a booking path a later initiative needs. Section 4.5 lists them with their funding routes; owners and start dates are proposals for Steerco to confirm.

**Seats and season, from 2027 H1.** Air Access holds winter seats with demand through joint green-season marketing with carriers on the full routes (I6, I2). It also tracks the runway programme quarterly and models capacity against demand to 2035 (I6). The Convention Bureau publishes a green-season events calendar and aims bids at May to September (I2).

**Governance and baselines, from 2027 H1.** The Wesgro CEO's office and DEDAT constitute Steerco and table the first national escalation agenda (I15, I17). Research agrees the data-sharing protocol with ACSA, SA Tourism, Stats SA and Cape Town Tourism (I16). It also runs a bookability census of provincial product by district (I3) and requests visitor counts and capacity from the five flagship sites (I11). DEDAT, with Wesgro Research, commissions the tourism labour analysis behind the jobs ambition (I18).

**Product and inclusion, from 2027 H2.** Tourism packages the Garden Route and Route 62 with a shuttle transfer sold inside the itinerary (I8, I9), and the Southern Line as a visitor product with the City and PRASA (I8). It chooses two or three pilot communities and agrees who funds a seller with a stake in each (I12). From 2028 H1, the LTOs, with Tourism, give each pilot community one live booking route before any promotion (I12, I3).
How progress will be measured

Seven impact indicators, twenty-five outcome indicators and thirty-six output indicators measure the plan. Steerco receives a quarterly scorecard, and the Board an annual outlook against both paths. Gates at the end of 2028 and 2031, a mid-term review in 2030 and a terminal evaluation in 2035 decide what each phase funds.

blocks.text: The main risks

The risks that matter most sit outside Wesgro's control, so the response is early warning and a route to the tier that can act. Restrictive bilateral air agreements and the US carrier cap are the one risk rated high on both likelihood and impact. The response is an escalation agenda with stated asks and route work inside existing rights.

Three risks are rated medium likelihood and high impact. If runway relief at Cape Town International slips past about 2033, the response is quarterly milestone tracking, more frequency and larger aircraft, with George for domestic connections. If visa processing for growth markets does not improve, the escalation agenda carries it and processing time is tracked each year. Safety incidents or perception that deter visitors meet safety gates before pilot launches and escalation to SAPS. Climate events that close sites and routes are rated high likelihood and medium impact; a climate risk register and itineraries routed around closures are the response. Likelihood and impact are Letsema's assessment, and section 4.8 holds the full register.
What Steerco and the Board are asked to decide
The Wesgro Board decides:

items: Adopt growth to 2.5 million arrivals by 2035 as the plan's goal, with the base and accelerated paths as its targets.

Constitute the Tourism Growth Steerco, co-chaired by Wesgro's CEO and DEDAT's Head of Department with Cape Town Tourism as a standing member, and confirm the twelve initiative leads that sit with Wesgro.

Approve the nine first-24-month actions that sit inside Wesgro's mandate and budget. Ask Wesgro Finance and DEDAT to set rand bands for every initiative, and to name what Wesgro deprioritises to fund them, before Gate 1. [Open item: Wesgro Finance to give an indicative rand band for the first 24 months.]
Commission the bookability census in 2027, so the plan's missing baselines exist by Gate 1.
Table the first national escalation agenda on visas, air service agreements and immigration processing at Cape Town International.

blocks.text: The Board recommends to the Provincial Minister, DEDAT and the municipalities:

items: That DEDAT commission the tourism labour analysis in 2027 and lead I10, I13 and I18, and that the Department of Mobility lead I8.
That the municipalities and LTOs lead and fund I12, and that the site operators lead I11.
